cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite equiprobable sample space whose elementary outcomes are unordered k-subsets of n distinct objects without replacement, the denominator has binomial-coefficient size n choose k.
major_error_concepts: Using n choose k when order changes the outcome, replacement is allowed, or the k-subsets are not equiprobable.
cards.prompt: Define Unordered equiprobable sample-space count. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The elementary outcomes are unordered k-subsets of n distinct objects without replacement.
Their count is the binomial coefficient n choose k.
The count is a probability denominator only when those unordered outcomes are equiprobable.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The consequences P(A complement)=1-P(A) and A subset B implies P(A)<=P(B).
major_error_concepts: Subtracting from 100 while mixing percentage and probability units.
cards.prompt: Define Complement and monotonicity identities. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The consequences P(A complement)=1-P(A) and A subset B implies P(A)<=P(B).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The first-course consequence that probabilities of increasing unions converge upward and decreasing intersections converge downward under the standard probability-space contract.
major_error_concepts: Reversing set inclusion or claiming finite equality at some unspecified n.
cards.prompt: Define Continuity of event probabilities. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Probabilities of increasing unions converge upward.
Probabilities of decreasing intersections converge downward under the standard probability-space contract.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It controls the probability of at least one event in a finite or countable family by summing marginal probabilities, without needing independence, but it may be loose when events overlap.
major_error_concepts: Treating the upper bound as an exact probability or assuming independence.
cards.prompt: What is Countable union bound used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It upper-bounds a finite or countable union by a probability sum.
Overlap can make the bound loose.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The adversarial check that enumerated outcomes are exhaustive mutually distinguishable and assigned weights justified by the physical or generative model.
major_error_concepts: Repairing an inconvenient result by changing the sample space after seeing it.
cards.prompt: Define equiprobable-model validity condition.
required_concepts: The adversarial check that enumerated outcomes are exhaustive mutually distinguishable and assigned weights justified by the physical or generative model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A finite or countable family of pairwise disjoint events whose union is the sample space, used for exhaustive case analysis.
major_error_concepts: Calling overlapping cases a partition and double counting their overlap.
cards.prompt: Define Event partition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A finite or countable family of pairwise disjoint events whose union is the sample space, used for exhaustive case analysis.

cards.definition: **Definition.** union intersection complement and difference as logical or and not operations relative to one declared sample space.
major_error_concepts: Taking a complement without declaring the ambient sample space.
cards.prompt: Define Event set operations. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: union intersection complement and difference as logical or and not operations relative to one declared sample space.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An event represented by a subset of the sample space and occurring exactly when the realized outcome lies in that subset.
major_error_concepts: Calling the numerical probability one half the event itself.
cards.prompt: Define Events as subsets. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An event represented by a subset of the sample space and occurring exactly when the realized outcome lies in that subset.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The special model in which each of N elementary outcomes has probability 1/N so event probability is favorable count divided by N.
major_error_concepts: Using favorable-over-total when the elementary outcomes have unequal probabilities.
cards.prompt: Define Finite equiprobable model. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The special model in which each of N elementary outcomes has probability 1/N so event probability is favorable count divided by N.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For a finite family of events under one probability measure, the probability of their union is the alternating sum of the probabilities of all nonempty intersections; it requires neither independence nor an equiprobable finite sample space.
major_error_concepts: Adding event probabilities without overlap corrections or claiming the formula requires independent events.
cards.prompt: Define Probability inclusion-exclusion formula. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The formula applies to a finite family of events under one probability measure.
It alternates sums of single-event probabilities and all higher-order intersection probabilities.
It requires neither independence nor equiprobable elementary outcomes.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The zero-one variable 1_A that equals one exactly on event A and converts set operations and counts into algebra.
major_error_concepts: Treating an indicator as the probability of its event rather than a realized zero-one value.
cards.prompt: Define Indicator random variable. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The zero-one variable 1_A that equals one exactly on event A and converts set operations and counts into algebra.

cards.definition: **Definition.** In a uniform sequence sample space, the type class with fixed category counts n1 through nr summing to n contains n!/(n1!...nr!) elementary outcomes, so its probability is that count divided by the total uniform sequence count.
major_error_concepts: Treating the multinomial type-class count as a probability by itself or using its favorable-over-total ratio when category sequences are not uniform.
cards.prompt: Define Equiprobable multinomial type-class count. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The probability application uses a uniform sequence sample space and a type class with fixed category counts summing to n.
The type-class count is n!/(n1!...nr!).
The type-class probability divides that count by the total number of uniform elementary sequences.

cards.definition: **Definition.** An occupancy counting model assigns objects to boxes after declaring whether objects and boxes are labeled, whether empty boxes or collisions are allowed, and whether capacities constrain the assignments.
major_error_concepts: Using stars and bars when labeled objects make assignments distinct or when occupancy constraints violate that model's assumptions.
cards.prompt: Define occupancy counting model. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: An occupancy model assigns objects to boxes.
The model declares whether the objects are labeled or unlabeled.
The model declares whether the boxes are labeled or unlabeled.
The model declares whether empty boxes and multiple objects in one box are allowed.
The model declares any capacity constraint on a box.

cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite equiprobable sample space whose elementary outcomes are ordered k-selections without replacement from n distinct objects, the denominator has falling-factorial size n!/(n-k)!.
major_error_concepts: Using an unordered subset count when different selection orders are distinct elementary outcomes.
cards.prompt: Define Ordered equiprobable sample-space count. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The elementary outcomes are ordered k-selections of n distinct objects without replacement.
Their count is the falling factorial n!/(n-k)!.
The count is a probability denominator only when those ordered outcomes are equiprobable.

cards.definition: **Definition.** nonnegativity normalization P(Omega)=1 and countable additivity on disjoint events as the defining probability-measure contract.
major_error_concepts: Treating empirical frequency alone as an axiomatically complete probability assignment.
cards.prompt: Define Probability axioms. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: nonnegativity normalization P(Omega)=1 and countable additivity on disjoint events as the defining probability-measure contract.

cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite equiprobable experiment built from successive stages, the elementary-outcome count is the product of the stagewise continuation counts when every partial outcome has the declared number of continuations; event probability is favorable count over that total only after equiprobability is justified.
major_error_concepts: Claiming every multistage probability denominator is the product of the stage sizes even when continuation counts depend on the partial outcome.
cards.prompt: Define Equiprobable product sample-space count. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The card applies the generic product rule only to a finite staged sample space whose continuation counts satisfy the stated uniformity condition.
The total elementary-outcome count is the product of the stagewise continuation counts.
Favorable-over-total is a probability formula only when the counted elementary outcomes are equiprobable.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set Omega of all mutually distinguishable elementary outcomes under the specified observation resolution.
major_error_concepts: Omitting possible outcomes because they do not belong to the target event.
cards.prompt: Define Sample space and outcome. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set Omega of all mutually distinguishable elementary outcomes under the specified observation resolution.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The model distinction that replacement preserves the item pool while no replacement changes later probabilities and induces dependence.
major_error_concepts: Using a binomial model for no-replacement sampling from a small finite population.
cards.prompt: Distinguish Sampling with versus without replacement.
required_concepts: With replacement, each selected item is returned, so the item pool and the next-draw probabilities remain unchanged.
Without replacement, a selected item is removed, so the item pool and later draw probabilities change and the draws are generally dependent.
The decisive boundary is whether one draw changes the sampling frame used by subsequent draws.

cards.definition: **Definition.** In a finite equiprobable sample space partitioned into disjoint cases, the favorable-outcome count is the sum of the case counts and its probability is that sum divided by the common total outcome count.
major_error_concepts: Adding counts for overlapping probability cases as though they were a partition.
cards.prompt: Define Equiprobable disjoint-case sample-space count. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The card applies the generic sum rule to disjoint cases inside one finite equiprobable sample space.
The favorable-outcome count is the sum of the disjoint case counts.
The probability ratio uses one common total and is invalid without equiprobable elementary outcomes.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** For events A_1,A_2,..., P(union_{i=1}^infinity A_i) <=sum_{i=1}^infinity P(A_i), without an independence assumption. The finite union bound is the finite-family special case.
major_error_concepts: Reporting 0.01 as the exact probability or assuming the events are disjoint.
cards.prompt: State the countable union bound, including its finite-family special case.
required_concepts: P(union_{i=1}^infinity A_i)<=sum_{i=1}^infinity P(A_i).
No independence assumption is required.
The finite union bound is the finite-family special case.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The check that a rare prior event can remain unlikely after a positive but imperfect test even when sensitivity is high.
major_error_concepts: Ignoring false positives from the large noncase population.
cards.prompt: Define Base-rate diagnostic. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The check that a rare prior event can remain unlikely after a positive but imperfect test even when sensitivity is high.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It reverses a conditional probability to infer a latent cause or hypothesis from observed evidence, combining likelihood with prior prevalence; the posterior still requires the full evidence normalization and is not the prior or false-positive rate alone.
major_error_concepts: Treating P(B given A) as P(A given B), or omitting prior prevalence and the full evidence normalization P(B).
cards.prompt: What is Bayes theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It reverses a conditional probability to infer a latent cause or hypothesis from observed evidence, combining likelihood with prior prevalence
the posterior still requires the full evidence normalization and is not the prior or false-positive rate alone.

cards.definition: Let A_1,...,A_m be a complete pairwise-disjoint partition with P(A_j)>0, and let evidence B satisfy P(B)>0. Then P(A_i|B)=P(B|A_i)P(A_i)/P(B), where P(B)=sum_j P(B|A_j)P(A_j). The likelihood and prior must be combined and normalized across all partition branches; P(B|A_i) is not generally P(A_i|B).
major_error_concepts: Reversing P(A_i|B) and P(B|A_i) without a valid special-case justification.
Omitting prior weights or the full evidence normalizer.
Applying the elementary ratio when P(B)=0.
cards.prompt: State Bayes theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: Use a complete disjoint positive-probability partition.
The evidence B has positive probability.
Posterior equals likelihood times prior divided by the full evidence probability.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The factorization within each specified condition, which need not imply marginal independence and is not established by pairwise conditional stories.
major_error_concepts: Dropping the conditioning variable from the factorization without justification.
cards.prompt: Define Conditional independence boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The factorization within each specified condition, which need not imply marginal independence and is not established by pairwise conditional stories.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The renormalized probability P(A given B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B) defined in the elementary event formula when P(B)>0.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by P(A) or using the formula when P(B)=0.
cards.prompt: Define Conditional probability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The renormalized probability P(A given B)=P(A intersection B)/P(B) defined in the elementary event formula when P(B)>0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The boundary that the elementary event ratio does not define conditioning on a probability-zero event and density or measure-aware methods need their own contracts.
major_error_concepts: Cancelling infinitesimals or treating density height as point probability.
cards.prompt: Define Conditioning on null events. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The elementary event-ratio formula does not define conditioning on a probability-zero event.
Density-based or measure-theoretic conditioning requires its own explicit contract.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The recognition that P(A given B) and P(B given A) differ and aggregated associations can reverse after stratification.
major_error_concepts: Swapping condition and target or interpreting an aggregate reversal causally.
cards.prompt: Define Conditioning reversal and Simpson diagnostic. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The recognition that P(A given B) and P(B given A) differ and aggregated associations can reverse after stratification.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction that disjoint positive-probability events have intersection probability zero and therefore are dependent.
major_error_concepts: Calling mutually exclusive events independent because they cannot influence one another.
cards.prompt: Distinguish Disjointness versus independence.
required_concepts: Disjoint events satisfy A intersect B=emptyset and therefore P(A intersect B)=0.
Independent events satisfy P(A intersect B)=P(A)P(B).
Two disjoint events with positive probabilities are dependent because 0=P(A intersect B) is not P(A)P(B)>0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction that permutation-invariant joint laws need not factorize into independent coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Calling symmetry under reordering proof of product factorization.
cards.prompt: Distinguish Exchangeability versus independence boundary.
required_concepts: Exchangeability means that the joint distribution is invariant under permutations of the coordinates.
Independence means that the joint distribution factorizes into the product of the coordinate marginal distributions.
Permutation invariance alone does not imply factorization, so exchangeable coordinates need not be independent.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The consequence that independence of A and B extends to complements and mixed complement pairs.
major_error_concepts: Assuming only the original pair factorizes while complement events must be dependent.
cards.prompt: Define Independence under complements. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The consequence that independence of A and B extends to complements and mixed complement pairs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The factorization P(A intersection B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently unchanged conditional probability when denominators are positive.
major_error_concepts: Declaring events independent because they sound unrelated without checking the model.
cards.prompt: Define Independent events. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The factorization P(A intersection B)=P(A)P(B), equivalently unchanged conditional probability when denominators are positive.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The model of fixed trial count common success probability and mutual trial independence leading to product-path probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Using the same expression when success probabilities change or trials are dependent.
cards.prompt: Define Independent repeated Bernoulli trials. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The model of fixed trial count common success probability and mutual trial independence leading to product-path probabilities.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It computes a marginal event probability by averaging branch-specific conditional probabilities over a complete partition and supplies the denominator in Bayes' theorem; missing or unweighted branches invalidate the result.
major_error_concepts: Omitting a partition branch or failing to weight conditional rates by branch probabilities.
cards.prompt: What is Law of total probability used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It computes a marginal event probability by averaging branch-specific conditional probabilities over a complete partition and supplies the denominator in Bayes' theorem
missing or unweighted branches invalidate the result.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The decomposition P(B)=sum_i P(B given A_i)P(A_i) over a complete positive-probability partition.
major_error_concepts: Omitting a partition branch or failing to weight conditional rates by branch probabilities.
cards.prompt: State Law of total probability, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The events A_1,...,A_n form a complete pairwise-disjoint partition of the sample space.
Each partition event used in the conditional probabilities has P(A_i)>0.
For any event B, P(B)=sum_i P(B given A_i)P(A_i).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The rearrangement P(A intersection B)=P(A given B)P(B) with the conditioning direction and positive denominator recorded.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying unrelated marginal probabilities without conditional or independence evidence.
cards.prompt: Define Multiplication rule. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The rearrangement P(A intersection B)=P(A given B)P(B) with the conditioning direction and positive denominator recorded.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that every finite subcollection factorizes, stronger than checking only all pairs.
major_error_concepts: Checking only P(A intersection B intersection C)=P(A)P(B)P(C).
cards.prompt: Define Mutual independence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that every finite subcollection factorizes, stronger than checking only all pairs.

cards.definition: **Definition.** On the uniform sample space {HH,HT,TH,TT}, let A={HH,HT}, B={HH,TH}, and C={HH,TT}. Every event has probability 1/2 and every pairwise intersection has probability 1/4, so the pairs are independent; however P(A intersect B intersect C)=1/4 rather than 1/8, so the three events are not mutually independent.
major_error_concepts: Assuming pairwise independence automatically extends to all intersections.
cards.prompt: What claim does Pairwise-not-mutual counterexample refute, and why?
required_concepts: The false claim is that pairwise independence of a collection implies mutual independence.
A concrete uniform construction is A={HH,HT}, B={HH,TH}, and C={HH,TT} on {HH,HT,TH,TT}.
Each event has probability 1/2 and each pairwise intersection has probability 1/4=(1/2)(1/2), so every pair is independent.
The triple intersection has probability 1/4 rather than (1/2)^3=1/8, so the collection is not mutually independent.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The multiplicative update posterior odds equals prior odds times likelihood ratio for a two-hypothesis event model.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying prior probability rather than prior odds by the likelihood ratio and calling the result a probability.
cards.prompt: Define Prior odds likelihood ratio and posterior odds. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The multiplicative update posterior odds equals prior odds times likelihood ratio for a two-hypothesis event model.
cards.term: Prior odds likelihood ratio and posterior odds

cards.definition: **Definition.** The branch representation whose path products give intersections and whose disjoint leaf sums give target events.
major_error_concepts: Adding branch probabilities along a path instead of multiplying.
cards.prompt: Define Probability tree. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The branch representation whose path products give intersections and whose disjoint leaf sums give target events.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The factorization of a joint event into a sequence of conditional probabilities under one ordered history.
major_error_concepts: Using the same 4/52 factor at every stage as though draws were replaced.
cards.prompt: Define Sequential chain rule. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The factorization of a joint event into a sequence of conditional probabilities under one ordered history.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The zero-one law with success probability p, expectation p, and variance p(1-p).
major_error_concepts: Using support {1,2} or reporting variance p.
cards.prompt: Define Bernoulli distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The zero-one law with success probability p, expectation p, and variance p(1-p).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The count of successes in n mutually independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p.
major_error_concepts: Using a binomial law for no-replacement draws with changing success probability.
cards.prompt: Define Binomial distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The count of successes in n mutually independent Bernoulli trials with common success probability p.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The right-continuous nondecreasing function F(x)=P(X<=x) whose jumps equal point masses.
major_error_concepts: Drawing a continuous line between jumps and creating mass where none exists.
cards.prompt: Define Discrete cumulative distribution function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The right-continuous nondecreasing function F(x)=P(X<=x) whose jumps equal point masses.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The rule E[g(X)]=sum_x g(x)p_X(x) when the expectation is well defined, without requiring a separate law of g(X).
major_error_concepts: Averaging distinct support values without probability weights.
cards.prompt: Define Discrete LOTUS. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The rule E[g(X)]=sum_x g(x)p_X(x) when the expectation is well defined, without requiring a separate law of g(X).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The probability assignment to values or measurable sets induced by the random-variable mapping and underlying outcome model.
major_error_concepts: Assuming equal probability for the three X values because there are three of them.
cards.prompt: Define Distribution or law. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The probability assignment to values or measurable sets induced by the random-variable mapping and underlying outcome model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The requirement that positive and negative contributions define the requested finite expectation rather than an undefined infinity-minus-infinity expression.
major_error_concepts: Manipulating a divergent series as though linearity guaranteed a finite answer.
cards.prompt: Define Expectation existence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The requirement that positive and negative contributions define the requested finite expectation rather than an undefined infinity-minus-infinity expression.

cards.definition: For independent Bernoulli trials with constant p in (0,1], the trials-until-first-success variable T has P(T=k)=(1-p)^(k-1)p for k=1,2,... and E[T]=1/p. The failures-before-success variable F=T-1 has P(F=k)=(1-p)^k p for k=0,1,... and E[F]=(1-p)/p. Both have variance (1-p)/p². At p=1 they are degenerate at 1 and 0 respectively.
major_error_concepts: A geometric variable supported on 0,1,... and counting failures has mean 1/p.
cards.prompt: State the two geometric waiting-time conventions, their PMFs, and how their means differ.
required_concepts: Declare which support convention is used.
Match the probability exponent and mean to that support.
Trials are independent with constant positive success probability.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The success count in a fixed number of draws without replacement from a finite population with category totals declared.
major_error_concepts: Using binomial p=(3/5) independently for both draws.
cards.prompt: Define Hypergeometric distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The success count in a fixed number of draws without replacement from a finite population with category totals declared.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The representation of a random count N=sum_i 1_{A_i} so E[N]=sum_i P(A_i) under expectation existence.
major_error_concepts: Using the probability of at least one match as the expected number of matching pairs.
cards.prompt: Define Indicator counting method. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The representation of a random count N=sum_i 1_{A_i} so E[N]=sum_i P(A_i) under expectation existence.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c whenever the involved expectations are valid, with no independence requirement.
major_error_concepts: Requiring the indicators to be independent before summing expectations.
cards.prompt: Define Linearity of expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The identity E[aX+bY+c]=aE[X]+bE[Y]+c whenever the involved expectations are valid, with no independence requirement.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The expectations E[X^k] and E[(X-E[X])^k] when finite, with raw and centered roles separated.
major_error_concepts: Calling every raw moment a central moment or assuming all orders exist.
cards.prompt: Define Moments and centered moments. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The expectations E[X^k] and E[(X-E[X])^k] when finite, with raw and centered roles separated.

cards.definition: For independent Bernoulli trials with fixed p in (0,1) and positive integer r, the number F of failures before the rth success has P(F=k)=choose(k+r-1,r-1) p^r(1-p)^k for k=0,1,... . The total-trials convention is T=F+r, supported on r,r+1,... . Thus E[F]=r(1-p)/p and E[T]=r/p. At p=1 the laws are degenerate at 0 and r. The distribution name is also extended to noninteger shape parameters in count models, a separate parameterization.
major_error_concepts: The number of trials until the rth success has support starting at zero and equals the failures count without any shift.
cards.prompt: Define the waiting-time negative-binomial law using the failures-before-rth-success convention and relate it to total trials.
required_concepts: State the independent constant-p trial model and positive integer r for waiting-time use.
Give the failures-count PMF and support.
The total-trials variable is shifted by r.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The reconstruction P(X in A)=sum over support values in A of p_X(x) with support and total mass audited.
major_error_concepts: Summing over integer values outside the declared support or forgetting an endpoint.
cards.prompt: Define PMF normalization and event sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The reconstruction P(X in A)=sum over support values in A of p_X(x) with support and total mass audited.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nonnegative-integer count law with rate parameter lambda over the specified exposure and PMF exp(-lambda)lambda^k/k!.
major_error_concepts: Treating lambda as a probability restricted below one or omitting its exposure units.
cards.prompt: Define Poisson distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nonnegative-integer count law with rate parameter lambda over the specified exposure and PMF exp(-lambda)lambda^k/k!.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nonnegative function p_X(x)=P(X=x) summing to one over discrete support.
major_error_concepts: Integrating PMF heights over intervals as though they were a density.
cards.prompt: Define Probability mass function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nonnegative function p_X(x)=P(X=x) summing to one over discrete support.

cards.definition: A real random variable is a measurable function X:Omega→R: the preimage of every Borel subset of R is an event. It maps each outcome to a number, may map multiple outcomes to the same number, and induces the law P_X(B)=P(X^{-1}(B)). In a finite sample space with every subset declared an event, measurability is automatic; it is not automatic in every probability model.
major_error_concepts: Every arbitrary function on every probability space is automatically a random variable, even if some Borel preimages are not events.
cards.prompt: Define Random variable as a mapping. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A random variable is a function on outcomes, not a single observed value.
Borel preimages must be events.
Its distribution is the induced probability law.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set of values with positive probability in a discrete law under the declared parameter range.
major_error_concepts: Including negative counts or omitting endpoints.
cards.prompt: Define Support. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set of values with positive probability in a discrete law under the declared parameter range.

cards.definition: **Definition.** variance E[(X-mu)^2]=E[X^2]-mu^2 when finite and standard deviation its nonnegative square root in original units.
major_error_concepts: Reporting variance in the original units or using E[X^2]-E[X].
cards.prompt: Define Variance and standard deviation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: variance E[(X-mu)^2]=E[X^2]-mu^2 when finite and standard deviation its nonnegative square root in original units.

cards.definition: If a transformation maps a region of positive X-probability to a single value c, the output law has an atom at c of at least that region's probability. In a standard atom-plus-density example, the remaining absolutely continuous input is transformed through suitable differentiable inverse branches with nonzero derivative, producing a continuous-density part. Mere continuity of the map elsewhere does not guarantee that the remaining law has a density; singular components are possible.
major_error_concepts: A transformation that is merely continuous outside one flat region always produces only an atom plus an ordinary density, with no further assumptions.
cards.prompt: Define Atom-plus-density transformation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A positive-probability collapsed region contributes point mass.
An ordinary density for the remaining component requires appropriate regular transformation assumptions.
An atom cannot be represented by an ordinary finite density height.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The law on [0,1] with density proportional to x^(alpha-1)(1-x)^(beta-1) for positive parameters.
major_error_concepts: Extending support to all positive reals like a gamma law.
cards.prompt: Define Beta distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The law on [0,1] with density proportional to x^(alpha-1)(1-x)^(beta-1) for positive parameters.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The real-line density 1/[pi(1+x^2)] whose mean and variance do not exist as ordinary finite moments.
major_error_concepts: Cancelling divergent positive and negative integrals and reporting zero.
cards.prompt: Define Cauchy heavy-tail example. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The real-line density 1/[pi(1+x^2)] whose mean and variance do not exist as ordinary finite moments.

cards.definition: A CDF is F(x)=P(X≤x), with limits 0 and 1 at the two infinities. It is continuous exactly when the law has no point masses. If the law is absolutely continuous with density f, then F(x)=integral_{-infinity}^x f(t)dt and F'=f almost everywhere. A continuous CDF can instead be singular, as with the Cantor distribution, and need not admit a density.
major_error_concepts: Every continuous CDF has an ordinary density and equals the integral of its derivative, including the Cantor distribution.
cards.prompt: Distinguish a continuous CDF from an absolutely continuous CDF, and state when density integration and differentiation apply.
required_concepts: Continuity of a CDF means absence of atoms.
An integral-of-density representation requires absolute continuity.
For that representation the derivative equality holds almost everywhere.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The integral E[g(X)]=integral g(x)f_X(x)dx over support when the expectation exists.
major_error_concepts: Integrating over all reals without applying the support indicator or density.
cards.prompt: Define Continuous LOTUS. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The integral E[g(X)]=integral g(x)f_X(x)dx over support when the expectation exists.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The property P(X>s+t given X>s)=P(X>t) for exponential waiting time with nonnegative s,t.
major_error_concepts: Using geometric integer support formulas without converting time and parameter conventions.
cards.prompt: Define Continuous memorylessness. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The property P(X>s+t given X>s)=P(X>t) for exponential waiting time with nonnegative s,t.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The distinction that an absolutely continuous variable has P(X=x)=0 even when f(x)>1 and that density carries reciprocal units.
major_error_concepts: Calling f(x) a point probability or rejecting every density value above one.
cards.prompt: Distinguish Density height versus point probability.
required_concepts: A density value f(x) is a height with reciprocal units and may exceed 1.
For an absolutely continuous random variable, the point probability P(X=x) is zero.
Probabilities are obtained by integrating the density over sets or intervals, not by treating f(x) as a point mass.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nonnegative waiting-time law with rate lambda and density lambda exp(-lambda x), mean 1/lambda.
major_error_concepts: Using scale 2 while labeling it rate 2.
cards.prompt: Define Exponential distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nonnegative waiting-time law with rate lambda and density lambda exp(-lambda x), mean 1/lambda.

cards.definition: In the shape-rate convention, Gamma(alpha,beta) has alpha>0, beta>0 and density beta^alpha x^(alpha-1) exp(-beta x)/Gamma(alpha) for x>0, zero elsewhere. Its mean is alpha/beta and variance alpha/beta². In the shape-scale convention theta=1/beta, those become alpha theta and alpha theta². Shape alpha=1 gives an exponential law with rate beta.
major_error_concepts: Gamma shape alpha and rate beta have mean alpha beta, and the same numeric rate and scale denote the same law.
cards.prompt: Define the gamma density in shape-rate form and translate its parameters and moments to shape-scale form.
required_concepts: State a normalized gamma density with positive shape and rate or scale.
Rate beta and scale theta are reciprocals.
Match the mean and variance to the declared convention.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The difference P(a<X<=b)=F(b)-F(a), adjusted for endpoint atoms when the law is not continuous.
major_error_concepts: Adding CDF values or reversing the subtraction.
cards.prompt: Define Interval probability from a CDF. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The difference P(a<X<=b)=F(b)-F(a), adjusted for endpoint atoms when the law is not continuous.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The support-aware CDF or absolute-derivative method for Y=g(X) when g is one-to-one on the specified support.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying by derivative 2 instead of the inverse absolute derivative 1/2.
cards.prompt: Define Monotone transformation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The support-aware CDF or absolute-derivative method for Y=g(X) when g is one-to-one on the specified support.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The aggregation over every preimage branch or a direct CDF method when g is not one-to-one.
major_error_concepts: Keeping only the positive square-root preimage.
cards.prompt: Define Nonmonotone transformation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The aggregation over every preimage branch or a direct CDF method when g is not one-to-one.

cards.definition: For mu in R and sigma>0, X~N(mu,sigma²) has density f(x)=exp(-(x-mu)²/(2sigma²))/(sigma sqrt(2pi)) for all real x. Its mean is mu and variance is sigma²; sigma is the standard deviation. Symmetry or a bell-shaped plot alone does not identify this law.
major_error_concepts: Every symmetric bell-shaped density is normal, and the second parameter sigma² is the standard deviation.
cards.prompt: Define N(mu,sigma²) by its density, support, and parameter meaning.
required_concepts: State the Gaussian exponential density and its normalizing factor.
Support is R, mu is real, and sigma>0.
Distinguish variance sigma² from standard deviation sigma.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The affine transform Z=(X-mu)/sigma producing a standard normal when X is normal with sigma>0.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by variance 4 rather than standard deviation 2.
cards.prompt: Define Normal standardization. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The affine transform Z=(X-mu)/sigma producing a standard normal when X is normal with sigma>0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** A nonnegative integrable function f with total integral one whose set probabilities are integrals, while density values themselves are not probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Checking only the total integral while allowing negative density on part of the support.
cards.prompt: Define Probability density function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: A nonnegative integrable function f with total integral one whose set probabilities are integrals, while density values themselves are not probabilities.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The generalized inverse locating the smallest x with F(x)>=p for p in (0,1), with nonuniqueness or jumps handled by convention.
major_error_concepts: Solving f(x)=0.5 using the density rather than F(x)=0.5.
cards.prompt: Define Quantile function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The generalized inverse locating the smallest x with F(x)>=p for p in (0,1), with nonuniqueness or jumps handled by convention.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity E[X]=integral_0^infinity P(X>t)dt for a nonnegative integrable random variable, with extended-value interpretation when divergent.
major_error_concepts: Applying the nonnegative identity directly to a signed variable without splitting parts.
cards.prompt: Define Tail integral identity. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The identity E[X]=integral_0^infinity P(X>t)dt for a nonnegative integrable random variable, with extended-value interpretation when divergent.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The constant-density law on a declared finite interval with probability proportional to subinterval length.
major_error_concepts: Using a discrete equal-mass model at every real point.
cards.prompt: Define Uniform distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The constant-density law on a declared finite interval with probability proportional to subinterval length.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The bilinear scaling and shift invariance Cov(aX+b,cY+d)=ac Cov(X,Y).
major_error_concepts: Adding b and d to the covariance value.
cards.prompt: Define Affine covariance rules. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The bilinear scaling and shift invariance Cov(aX+b,cY+d)=ac Cov(X,Y).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The normalized joint-density slice f(x,y)/f_Y(y) for conditioning values with positive marginal density under the first-course formula.
major_error_concepts: Calling the density value a point probability or conditioning at an unsupported y.
cards.prompt: Define Conditional PDF. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The normalized joint-density slice f(x,y)/f_Y(y) for conditioning values with positive marginal density under the first-course formula.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The normalized slice p(x,y)/p_Y(y) on values where p_Y(y)>0.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by p_X(0) rather than the probability of the conditioning value.
cards.prompt: Define Conditional PMF. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The normalized slice p(x,y)/p_Y(y) on values where p_Y(y)>0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The conditional-density integral g(y)=integral x f_(X given Y=y)(x)dx on valid conditioning values.
major_error_concepts: Integrating x against the joint density without dividing by f_Y(y).
cards.prompt: Define Continuous conditional expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The conditional-density integral g(y)=integral x f_(X given Y=y)(x)dx on valid conditioning values.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The unit-free covariance divided by positive standard deviations, defined only when both variances are finite and nonzero.
major_error_concepts: Computing correlation for a constant variable and dividing by zero standard deviation.
cards.prompt: Define Correlation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The unit-free covariance divided by positive standard deviations, defined only when both variances are finite and nonzero.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The centered product expectation Cov(X,Y)=E[(X-E X)(Y-E Y)] when second moments are finite.
major_error_concepts: Claiming zero covariance proves independence.
cards.prompt: Define Covariance. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The centered product expectation Cov(X,Y)=E[(X-E X)(Y-E Y)] when second moments are finite.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The function g(y)=sum_x x p(x given y), whose composition g(Y) is a random variable measurable with respect to Y at first-course depth.
major_error_concepts: Returning one unconditional scalar for every y.
cards.prompt: Define Discrete conditional expectation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The function g(y)=sum_x x p(x given y), whose composition g(Y) is a random variable measurable with respect to Y at first-course depth.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The equality of joint law to the product of marginals together with a compatible product support, for all relevant coordinate values.
major_error_concepts: Checking only one supported point where factorization happens accidentally.
cards.prompt: Define Joint independence factorization. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The equality of joint law to the product of marginals together with a compatible product support, for all relevant coordinate values.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nonnegative density whose integral over its support is one and whose region integrals give joint probabilities.
major_error_concepts: Integrating over the unit square and obtaining mass two.
cards.prompt: Define Joint PDF. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nonnegative density whose integral over its support is one and whose region integrals give joint probabilities.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The nonnegative mass p(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y) summing to one over the true discrete support.
major_error_concepts: Filling the missing fourth corner with mass one third and exceeding total probability one.
cards.prompt: Define Joint PMF. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The nonnegative mass p(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y) summing to one over the true discrete support.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The set where joint mass or density can be positive, including coupled constraints that control all marginal and conditional bounds.
major_error_concepts: Marginalizing with constant bounds zero to one for both variables.
cards.prompt: Define Joint support region. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The set where joint mass or density can be positive, including coupled constraints that control all marginal and conditional bounds.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It separates total variability into average within-group uncertainty and between-group variation of conditional means, clarifying where uncertainty comes from; the decomposition is in variances, not standard deviations.
major_error_concepts: Adding conditional standard deviations instead of variances.
cards.prompt: What is Law of total variance used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It separates total variability into average within-group uncertainty and between-group variation of conditional means, clarifying where uncertainty comes from
the decomposition is in variances, not standard deviations.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The decomposition Var(X)=E[Var(X given Y)]+Var(E[X given Y]) under finite second moment.
major_error_concepts: Adding conditional standard deviations instead of variances.
cards.prompt: State Law of total variance, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The random variable X has a finite second moment.
The within-group contribution is E[Var(X given Y)].
The between-group contribution is Var(E[X given Y]).
The conclusion is Var(X)=E[Var(X given Y)]+Var(E[X given Y)].

cards.definition: **Definition.** The laws obtained by summing or integrating the joint law over all valid values of the other coordinates.
major_error_concepts: Integrating y from zero to one and ignoring the triangular support.
cards.prompt: Define Marginal distributions. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The laws obtained by summing or integrating the joint law over all valid values of the other coordinates.

cards.definition: **Definition.** For a regular transformation Y=T(X), f_Y(y)=sum over regular x in T^{-1}(y) of f_X(x)/|det DT(x)| on the transformed support. If T is one-to-one, this reduces to f_X(T^{-1}(y))|det D(T^{-1})(y)|.
major_error_concepts: Using the forward determinant or leaving bounds in x,y coordinates.
cards.prompt: Define Random-vector transformation and Jacobian. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Sum f_X(x)/|det DT(x)| over all regular preimages x in T^{-1}(y).
For a one-to-one map use f_X(T^{-1}(y))|det D(T^{-1})(y)|.
Restrict the result to the transformed support.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The mapping from one outcome to an ordered tuple whose coordinate variables share one joint probability model.
major_error_concepts: Treating separately specified marginals as a complete joint law.
cards.prompt: Define Random vector. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The mapping from one outcome to an ordered tuple whose coordinate variables share one joint probability model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity E[E[X given Y]]=E[X] under integrability, with the inner object averaged over Y's law.
major_error_concepts: Averaging g(y) uniformly when Y is not uniform.
cards.prompt: Define Tower property. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The identity E[E[X given Y]]=E[X] under integrability, with the inner object averaged over Y's law.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The identity Var(sum_i X_i)=sum variances plus twice all pairwise covariances, reducing under pairwise uncorrelatedness.
major_error_concepts: Dropping covariance without independence or uncorrelatedness evidence.
cards.prompt: Define Variance of a sum. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The identity Var(sum_i X_i)=sum variances plus twice all pairwise covariances, reducing under pairwise uncorrelatedness.

cards.definition: Let X be uniform on {-1,0,1} and set Y=X². Then E[X]=0 and E[XY]=E[X³]=0, so Cov(X,Y)=0. They are not independent: P(Y=0|X=0)=1 whereas P(Y=0)=1/3. Thus finite-moment zero covariance does not imply independence, even when one variable is a deterministic function of the other.
major_error_concepts: X and X² are independent in this example because their covariance is zero.
cards.prompt: Give and verify a concrete pair with zero covariance but dependence.
required_concepts: Give an explicit joint model with the finite moments needed to define covariance: E|X|, E|Y|, and E|XY|.
Compute or otherwise establish zero covariance.
Demonstrate a specific failure of independence; the reference X,X² model is only one possible witness.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The result that the sum of n independent common-p Bernoulli variables is Binomial(n,p).
major_error_concepts: Using the closure when p varies by trial or trials are dependent.
cards.prompt: Define Binomial closure from Bernoulli sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The result that the sum of n independent common-p Bernoulli variables is Binomial(n,p).

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It controls cross-moments and covariance-like terms by separate second moments, supporting integrability, correlation, and convergence bounds; both variables need the stated square-integrability.
major_error_concepts: Using the result when a second moment is infinite.
cards.prompt: What is Cauchy-Schwarz expectation inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It controls cross-moments and covariance-like terms by separate second moments, supporting integrability, correlation, and convergence bounds
both variables need the stated square-integrability.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The bound abs(E[XY])<=sqrt(E[X^2]E[Y^2]) for square-integrable variables.
major_error_concepts: Using the result when a second moment is infinite.
cards.prompt: State Cauchy-Schwarz expectation inequality, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The random variables X and Y are square-integrable, so E[X^2] and E[Y^2] are finite.
The conclusion is abs(E[XY])<=sqrt(E[X^2]E[Y^2]).

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It turns a finite variance into a distribution-free deviation bound and is a basic route to weak-law arguments; it is often loose and does not describe the exact tail probability.
major_error_concepts: Using standard deviation in the numerator or forgetting the squared threshold.
cards.prompt: What is Chebyshev inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It turns a finite variance into a distribution-free deviation bound and is a basic route to weak-law arguments
it is often loose and does not describe the exact tail probability.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The variance-based bound P(abs(X-mu)>=a)<=Var(X)/a^2 for finite variance and a>0.
major_error_concepts: Using standard deviation in the numerator or forgetting the squared threshold.
cards.prompt: State Chebyshev inequality, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The random variable X has finite variance and mean mu=E[X].
The deviation threshold a is strictly positive.
The conclusion is P(abs(X-mu)>=a)<=Var(X)/a^2.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The integral f_Z(z)=integral f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)dx over overlap determined by both supports for independent continuous variables.
major_error_concepts: Integrating from zero to one for every z without enforcing z-x in [0,1].
cards.prompt: Define Continuous convolution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The integral f_Z(z)=integral f_X(x)f_Y(z-x)dx over overlap determined by both supports for independent continuous variables.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The sum over all support pairs p_Z(z)=sum_x p_X(x)p_Y(z-x) for independent discrete X,Y.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying equal-value probabilities instead of summing all pairs producing z.
cards.prompt: Define Discrete convolution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The sum over all support pairs p_Z(z)=sum_x p_X(x)p_Y(z-x) for independent discrete X,Y.

cards.definition: Let X_1,...,X_n be independent with a_i≤X_i≤b_i almost surely, and let D=sum_i(b_i-a_i)²>0. For t>0, P(sum_i(X_i-E[X_i])≥t)≤exp(-2t²/D). Applying the bound to both signs gives P(|sum_i(X_i-E[X_i])|≥t)≤2exp(-2t²/D), optionally capped at 1. Identical distributions are not required; if D=0 the centered sum is identically zero.
major_error_concepts: Independent finite-variance unbounded variables satisfy the same Hoeffding range bound by substituting their variances for (b_i-a_i)².
cards.prompt: State a Hoeffding tail bound for a centered sum of independent bounded variables.
required_concepts: The variables are independent and have declared almost-sure finite ranges.
Use the centered sum and denominator sum of squared range lengths.
One-sided exponent is -2t²/D; a two-sided bound may add the factor 2.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It compares transforming an average with averaging a transformed variable, underpinning moment, risk, entropy, and optimization bounds; convexity and integrability determine the direction and validity.
major_error_concepts: Reversing the inequality or using a concave function without changing direction.
cards.prompt: What is Jensen inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It compares transforming an average with averaging a transformed variable, underpinning moment, risk, entropy, and optimization bounds
convexity and integrability determine the direction and validity.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** Let phi be convex on a convex domain containing the range of an integrable X, with phi(X) integrable in the finite-valued form. Then phi(E[X])<=E[phi(X)].
major_error_concepts: Reversing the inequality or using a concave function without changing direction.
cards.prompt: State Jensen inequality, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: phi is convex on a convex domain containing the range of X.
X and phi(X) satisfy the stated integrability conditions.
The inequality is phi(E[X])<=E[phi(X)].

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It converts a nonnegative expectation into an upper-tail bound and provides the primitive step behind many moment and Chernoff inequalities; it does not apply directly to signed variables or yield an exact probability.
major_error_concepts: Applying the inequality directly to a signed X or reporting the bound as exact.
cards.prompt: What is Markov inequality used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It converts a nonnegative expectation into an upper-tail bound and provides the primitive step behind many moment and Chernoff inequalities
it does not apply directly to signed variables or yield an exact probability.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** The bound P(X>=a)<=E[X]/a for nonnegative X and a>0, with extended but useful cases qualified.
major_error_concepts: Applying the inequality directly to a signed X or reporting the bound as exact.
cards.prompt: State Markov inequality, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The random variable X is nonnegative.
The threshold a is strictly positive.
The conclusion is P(X>=a)<=E[X]/a; when E[X] is infinite the extended-real inequality is valid but noninformative.

cards.definition: If an MGF M_X(t)=E[e^(tX)] is finite on a neighborhood of 0, then M_X^(k)(0)=E[X^k]. For a nonnegative-integer variable with the relevant finite moments, its PGF G_X(s)=E[s^X] gives G_X'(1-)=E[X] and G_X''(1-)=E[X(X-1)], so E[X²]=G_X''(1-)+G_X'(1-). Finite PGF derivatives at 1 do not require an MGF finite for positive t.
major_error_concepts: The PGF second derivative at 1 equals E[X²], and any finite PGF derivative forces the MGF to exist around zero.
cards.prompt: How are raw moments extracted from an MGF and the first two factorial moments from a PGF? How do the latter recover E[X²]?
required_concepts: MGF derivatives at zero give raw moments under neighborhood finiteness.
PGF derivatives at 1 from below give factorial moments.
Add the first factorial moment to the second to recover E[X²].

cards.definition: **Definition.** The transform M_X(t)=E[exp(tX)] on the set where finite, with a neighborhood of zero required for standard uniqueness claims.
major_error_concepts: Assuming the MGF is finite for every real t and every distribution.
cards.prompt: Define Moment generating function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The transform M_X(t)=E[exp(tX)] on the set where finite, with a neighborhood of zero required for standard uniqueness claims.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The result that a sum of independent Poisson variables has rate equal to the sum of rates.
major_error_concepts: Adding rates without independence or mixing exposure units.
cards.prompt: Define Poisson addition closure. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The result that a sum of independent Poisson variables has rate equal to the sum of rates.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The power series G_X(s)=E[s^X] for nonnegative-integer X on its convergence domain, with coefficients equal to masses.
major_error_concepts: Using a PGF for a general signed continuous variable as though its coefficients were a PMF.
cards.prompt: Define Probability generating function. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The power series G_X(s)=E[s^X] for nonnegative-integer X on its convergence domain, with coefficients equal to masses.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The analysis of S=sum_{i=1}^N X_i by conditioning on the random count N and stating independence and integrability assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Replacing random N by E[N] inside the sum without a conditioning argument.
cards.prompt: Define Random sums by conditioning. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The analysis of S=sum_{i=1}^N X_i by conditioning on the random count N and stating independence and integrability assumptions.

cards.definition: For a finite sum S=sum_i X_i of integrable variables, E[S]=sum_i E[X_i] whether or not they are independent. With finite second moments, Var(S)=sum_i Var(X_i)+2sum_{i<j}Cov(X_i,X_j); independence makes those covariances zero. Under independence, MGFs or PGFs multiply on their common finite domain. Mentioning independence in a valid special case is not itself an error.
major_error_concepts: Claiming independence is necessary for mean additivity.
Dropping nonzero covariance terms without justification.
Multiplying transforms under dependence without a special reason.
cards.prompt: Define Sums of independent variables. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Mean additivity follows from integrability and linearity without requiring independence.
Variance additivity needs zero covariances, for which independence is sufficient.
Independent-sum transform products require a common valid domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The explicit interval or set of transform parameters for which the defining expectation is finite.
major_error_concepts: Writing a formal integral and differentiating it despite divergence.
cards.prompt: Define transform finiteness domain.
required_concepts: The explicit interval or set of transform parameters for which the defining expectation is finite.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The product rule for PGFs or MGFs of independent summands on a common valid domain.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying transforms under dependence or outside their finite domains.
cards.prompt: Define Transform of an independent sum. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The product rule for PGFs or MGFs of independent summands on a common valid domain.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The control of any of many bad events by summing individual probabilities without independence.
major_error_concepts: Multiplying complements as though the errors were independent.
cards.prompt: Define Union-bound tail control. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The control of any of many bad events by summing individual probabilities without independence.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The event that sample paths satisfy X_n(omega)->X(omega) for all outcomes except a probability-zero set, with formal measure details handed downstream.
major_error_concepts: Calling high probability at each n the same as one event of eventual path convergence.
cards.prompt: Define Almost-sure convergence intuition. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The event that sample paths satisfy X_n(omega)->X(omega) for all outcomes except a probability-zero set, with formal measure details handed downstream.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Central-limit convergence does not itself provide a finite-sample approximation-error bound; any quantitative finite-sample guarantee needs a separate theorem and its additional assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Reading a limiting statement as an exact finite-sample tolerance.
cards.prompt: Define Central-limit approximation-error boundary. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The central limit theorem's convergence statement does not itself provide a finite-sample error bound.
A quantitative finite-sample guarantee requires a separate theorem and its additional assumptions.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It justifies normal approximation for properly centered and scaled sums or averages and supports approximate uncertainty calculations; it is an asymptotic distributional result, not a claim that the raw finite sum is exactly standard normal.
major_error_concepts: Saying the unscaled sum converges to a standard normal.
cards.prompt: What is Central limit theorem used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It justifies normal approximation for properly centered and scaled sums or averages and supports approximate uncertainty calculations
it is an asymptotic distributional result, not a claim that the raw finite sum is exactly standard normal.

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If X_i are iid with finite mean mu and variance sigma^2 in (0,infinity), then (sum_{i=1}^n X_i-n mu)/(sigma sqrt(n)) converges in distribution to N(0,1).
major_error_concepts: Saying the unscaled sum converges to a standard normal.
cards.prompt: State Central limit theorem, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The X_i are iid with finite mean mu and variance sigma^2 in (0,infinity).
The centered sum is normalized by sigma sqrt(n).
The normalized sum converges in distribution to N(0,1).

cards.definition: **Definition.** The calculation Var(Xbar_n)=sigma^2/n followed by a Chebyshev bound tending to zero under iid finite variance.
major_error_concepts: Using variance sigma^2 rather than sigma^2/n after averaging independent terms.
cards.prompt: Define Chebyshev proof of a WLLN case. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The calculation Var(Xbar_n)=sigma^2/n followed by a Chebyshev bound tending to zero under iid finite variance.
cards.term: Chebyshev proof of a WLLN case

cards.definition: **Definition.** The half-unit adjustment when approximating an integer-lattice count event with a continuous normal variable.
major_error_concepts: Applying a continuity correction to an already continuous variable.
cards.prompt: Define Continuity correction. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The half-unit adjustment when approximating an integer-lattice count event with a continuous normal variable.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The convergence of CDFs at continuity points of the limit CDF, weaker than probability convergence in general.
major_error_concepts: Claiming the standardized sums approach one common random variable in probability.
cards.prompt: Define Convergence in distribution. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The convergence of CDFs at continuity points of the limit CDF, weaker than probability convergence in general.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The condition P(abs(X_n-X)>epsilon)->0 for every epsilon>0.
major_error_concepts: Checking only that E[X_n]->E[X].
cards.prompt: Define Convergence in probability. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The condition P(abs(X_n-X)>epsilon)->0 for every epsilon>0.

cards.definition: **Definition.** counterexamples or bounded interface demonstrating that weaker convergence modes do not generally recover stronger ones.
major_error_concepts: Using different probability spaces without stating how comparison variables are coupled.
cards.prompt: Define Failed-converse diagnostics. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: counterexamples or bounded interface demonstrating that weaker convergence modes do not generally recover stronger ones.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The valid implications almost sure to probability and mean square to probability, and probability to distribution, without asserting every converse.
major_error_concepts: Drawing a single two-way equivalence arrow among all modes.

required_concepts: The valid implications almost sure to probability and mean square to probability, and probability to distribution, without asserting every converse.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The condition E[(X_n-X)^2]->0, which implies convergence in probability by Markov or Chebyshev.
major_error_concepts: Calling convergence of variance sufficient when bias does not vanish.
cards.prompt: Define Mean-square convergence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The condition E[(X_n-X)^2]->0, which implies convergence in probability by Markov or Chebyshev.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The random sample average of simulated function values under a declared target distribution, whose bias variance and convergence depend on the simulation model.
major_error_concepts: Calling the estimate exact because the pseudorandom seed is fixed.
cards.prompt: Define Monte Carlo estimator. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The random sample average of simulated function values under a declared target distribution, whose bias variance and convergence depend on the simulation model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The square-root variance scale of a sample-average estimator, estimated from draws only under appropriate independence and finite-variance assumptions.
major_error_concepts: Claiming error shrinks as 1/n or ignoring serial dependence.
cards.prompt: Define Monte Carlo standard error. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The square-root variance scale of a sample-average estimator, estimated from draws only under appropriate independence and finite-variance assumptions.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The finite-n approximation obtained by translating a sum event to standardized coordinates and evaluating a normal CDF with qualification.
major_error_concepts: Using the CLT when np or n(1-p) is tiny without qualification.
cards.prompt: Define Normal approximation to sums. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The finite-n approximation obtained by translating a sum event to standardized coordinates and evaluating a normal CDF with qualification.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The statistic Xbar_n=(1/n)sum_i Xi whose randomness dependence and moment behavior derive from the full joint model.
major_error_concepts: Calling the sample mean equal to mu for every realized sample.
cards.prompt: Define Sample mean. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The statistic Xbar_n=(1/n)sum_i Xi whose randomness dependence and moment behavior derive from the full joint model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The centered and scaled quantity (sum_i Xi-nmu)/(sigma sqrt(n)) for iid finite positive variance variables.
major_error_concepts: Dividing by n sigma or omitting centering.
cards.prompt: Define Standardized sum. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The centered and scaled quantity (sum_i Xi-nmu)/(sigma sqrt(n)) for iid finite positive variance variables.

cards.definition: **Theorem role.** It establishes consistency of sample averages in probability and formalizes stabilization under repeated sampling; it does not imply monotone realized errors, eventual equality, or almost-sure convergence without a stronger law.
major_error_concepts: Claiming eventual exact equality or monotone decrease of realized error.
cards.prompt: What is Weak law of large numbers used for, and what is its main limitation?
required_concepts: It establishes consistency of sample averages in probability and formalizes stabilization under repeated sampling
it does not imply monotone realized errors, eventual equality, or almost-sure convergence without a stronger law.
cards.term: Weak law of large numbers: role

cards.definition: **Theorem statement.** If X_i are iid with finite mean mu and finite variance, then the sample mean converges in probability to mu. The finite-variance assumption matches the first-course Chebyshev proof route used here.
major_error_concepts: Claiming eventual exact equality or monotone decrease of realized error.
cards.prompt: State Weak law of large numbers, including its hypotheses and conclusion.
required_concepts: The X_i are iid with finite mean mu and finite variance.
The sample mean converges in probability to mu.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The WLLN states that the sample mean converges to mu in probability: for every epsilon>0, P(|Xbar_n-mu|>epsilon) tends to 0. The SLLN states that the sample mean converges to mu almost surely: P(lim_n Xbar_n=mu)=1. The stronger almost-sure conclusion requires a separate theorem and proof beyond the elementary Chebyshev WLLN argument.
major_error_concepts: Renaming convergence in probability as almost sure because both approach mu.
cards.prompt: How do the weak and strong laws of large numbers differ in their convergence claims, and what proof boundary separates them?
required_concepts: The WLLN gives convergence in probability: for every epsilon>0, P(|Xbar_n-mu|>epsilon) tends to 0.
The SLLN gives almost-sure convergence: P(lim_n Xbar_n=mu)=1.
The SLLN conclusion is stronger and requires a separate theorem and proof beyond the elementary Chebyshev WLLN argument.
cards.term: Weak versus strong law of large numbers

cards.definition: **Definition.** The finite-n approximation motivated by a limit theorem with normalization assumptions and error limitations retained.
major_error_concepts: Calling the limiting normal law the exact finite-n distribution.
cards.prompt: Define Asymptotic-approximation evidence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The finite-n approximation motivated by a limit theorem with normalization assumptions and error limitations retained.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The boundary that measure-aware conditioning martingales stochastic processes advanced concentration and limit theory require downstream foundations.

required_concepts: The boundary that measure-aware conditioning martingales stochastic processes advanced concentration and limit theory require downstream foundations.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The fully normalized finite sum or integral under the specified law that directly equals the requested event probability.
major_error_concepts: Calling a Monte Carlo frequency exact because many draws were used.
cards.prompt: Define Exact-probability evidence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The fully normalized finite sum or integral under the specified law that directly equals the requested event probability.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The check that rate scale variance standard deviation geometric support and count exposure conventions match across every evidence object.

required_concepts: The check that rate scale variance standard deviation geometric support and count exposure conventions match across every evidence object.

cards.definition: **Definition.** Changing an event definition, distribution, threshold, or independence assumption after inspecting a desired result creates a new probability model; the original calculation does not validate that new model, and inferential correction belongs to a downstream statistics analysis.
major_error_concepts: Reporting a probability obtained after changing the model in response to the result as if it came from the original prespecified model.
cards.prompt: Define Post-result probability-model change diagnostic. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: Changing an event definition, distribution, threshold, or independence assumption after seeing the result creates a newly specified probability model.
The original probability calculation does not validate the new model; any inferential correction requires separate downstream justification.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The boundary that a probability model derives consequences from a specified law while statistics uses data to learn or assess unknown aspects of a model.
major_error_concepts: Using mathematical correctness as empirical model validation.
cards.prompt: Define Probability versus statistical inference. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The boundary that a probability model derives consequences from a specified law while statistics uses data to learn or assess unknown aspects of a model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The seeded empirical distribution or frequency with Monte Carlo uncertainty, useful for checking implementation but not proving the source model.
major_error_concepts: Treating agreement to three decimals as proof that assumptions hold in real data.
cards.prompt: Define Simulation evidence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The seeded empirical distribution or frequency with Monte Carlo uncertainty, useful for checking implementation but not proving the source model.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The check that exact approximate and simulated calculations refer to the same outcome set support boundaries atoms and total probability one.
major_error_concepts: Comparing a density-only approximation with simulation that includes a censored atom.
cards.prompt: Define Support and normalization reconciliation. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The check that exact approximate and simulated calculations refer to the same outcome set support boundaries atoms and total probability one.

cards.definition: **Definition.** The theorem-qualified inequality that constrains but generally does not equal the target probability.
major_error_concepts: Comparing a loose upper bound numerically as though it were an estimate.
cards.prompt: Define Upper-or-lower-bound evidence. Include its essential conditions and distinctions.
required_concepts: The theorem-qualified inequality that constrains but generally does not equal the target probability.
